title: Speak or be silent
hookLine: when together, talk about the teaching or keep noble silence (MN 26)
last: PISUNA VACA — A SENTENCE THAT MENDS.

cards: Evening, outside a hermitage near Savatthi. The Buddha is standing at a closed door, waiting. Inside, a group of his monks are deep in conversation about the teaching.
He could walk straight in. They'd stop mid-sentence and bow, and the whole room would turn toward him. Instead he stays on the step, in the evening light, and lets them finish.
Only when the talk has come to its end does he clear his throat and knock. It's a quiet moment, and it opens a long sutta.

teach.b: The sutta is the Noble Search, in the Middle Length Discourses.
The monks had been hoping to hear a talk from the Buddha himself, and Ananda brought him to the hermitage of a brahmin named Rammaka, where they were gathered.
When the door opens, the Buddha sits down, asks what they were discussing, and approves. Then he gives them a rule of thumb short enough to remember for life.
When you gather together, he says, do one of two things: discuss the teaching, or keep noble silence. Two options, and everything else falls away.
Look at what this does to idle chatter, the fourth guard. It isn't fought with a ban. It's crowded out.

If you're not talking about what matters, you can simply be quiet together, and that quiet has a name: ariya tuṇhībhāva, noble silence. Not sulking, not awkwardness, not waiting for your turn to talk.
A chosen stillness, shared. Elsewhere in the canon, Moggallana gives noble silence a deeper meaning: a level of meditation where even thinking falls still.
Modern retreats borrow the phrase for days spent without talking at all. Both point the same direction. And look at what the Buddha does first.
He doesn't interrupt a good conversation, even one he could improve.
Then he speaks. The long sutta that follows is full of his own story: leaving home, his teachers, his awakening. It begins with a man waiting quietly on a step.

how: Many Buddhist retreats keep noble silence for their whole length, with talk only for teaching interviews and practical needs; some monasteries keep silence at meals or through the night until morning.

o: the silent treatment after an argument
a vow never to speak again
noble silence: a quiet chosen and shared

games.q: at Rammaka's hermitage: tap the pairs.
p: the brahmin whose hermitage it was
discuss the teaching, or noble silence

s: the Buddha interrupted the monks to set them straight
he stood outside until their talk ended, then cleared his throat and knocked.
in the canon, noble silence can also mean a meditation where thinking falls still
in SN 21.1 Moggallana calls the second jhāna noble silence.
it's a chosen, shared stillness, not avoidance.

games.q: you're the Buddha, outside the door. inside, your monks are mid-conversation about the teaching. what do you do?
o: walk in; they'll want to hear you.
wait until they finish, then knock.
leave quietly; they don't need you.
games.why: in MN 26 he stands outside until the talk ends, then clears his throat and knocks, and afterward praises them for discussing the teaching.

practice: For these two minutes, practice the second option. The voice in your head may keep talking, but you don't have to answer it.
Notice how much of it is chatter, rehearsing, commenting, narrating, and each time you catch it, come back to the breath, the way you'd step back into a quiet room.

wordCard.voice: Ariya tunhibhava, noble silence. The Buddha's rule for gathering: talk about what matters, or keep noble silence.

orig.note: Pali ariya tuṇhībhāva: noble silence, one of the two things to do when monks gather.

carryVoice: Your line: a chosen stillness, shared. When people gather, there are two good options. Day three hundred seventy, and counting.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 26 (Ariyapariyesana Sutta, the noble search)
Samyutta Nikaya 21.1 (Kolita Sutta, noble silence as the second jhana)
